VIDEO.title: Matthew 14:22-36 – Why Jesus Walked on Water (It’s Not What You Think)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 14:22-36. Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain to pray. In the fourth watch of the night He comes to them walking on the sea. Peter asks to come to Him on the water, walks, sees the wind, sinks, and is caught. The disciples worship Him, saying, 'You are truly God's Son!' At Gennesaret the sick are healed by touching the fringe of His garment.

Why the hurry? John explains: after the feeding the people said, 'This is truly the Prophet,' and were about to take Him by force to make Him king (John 6:14-15). Jesus sends the disciples away and withdraws.

The boat is 'battered,' a word that literally means tormented. Jesus says, 'it is I,' the same self-identification as God's 'I AM' (Exodus 3:14). The video argues Peter's 'if' means 'since': not a test of Jesus' identity but a request to do what his Rabbi does.

The scene retells the Exodus: Moses tells the people not to fear and God splits the sea (Exodus 14); Psalm 77 says God's way was in the sea; Job 9:8 says God alone 'tramples down the waves of the sea.' Jesus is the new Moses and also the God who controls the water.
Peter is afraid of the wind, not the water, and doubts, like the double-minded man of James 1. The lesson: Jesus expects His students to trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives.
QUOTES: Lord, since it is you, please enable me to do the same thing you are doing.
Jesus is also the God who controls the water.
Jesus expects his students to trust him and what he's doing in and through their lives.
Every disciple wants to be like their teacher.

LSB_QUOTES.text: But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid.”
And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and took hold of him, and *said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
Who alone stretches out the heavens / And tramples down the waves of the sea;

src.text: Therefore when the people saw the sign which He had done, they were saying, “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.” So Jesus, knowing that they were going to come and take Him by force to make Him king, withdrew again to the mountain by Himself alone.

lines.text: 'Immediately He made the disciples get into the boat' (14:22). John explains the urgency: the crowd drew the right conclusion from Deuteronomy 18 but wanted to crown Him by force.
Jesus dismisses the crowd and goes up the mountain alone to pray.

src.text: But the boat was already many stadia away from the land, being battered by the waves; for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night He came to them, walking on the sea.

lines.text: The word for 'battered' literally means tormented. The video says it describes demonic hostility in Matthew 8 and Revelation 9:5.
Earlier the video noted that Jews linked the sea with the watery chaos of Genesis 1:2, and that at 8:26 Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea.
The fourth watch is about 3 to 6 in the morning; they had been rowing most of the night.

STORM.title: It is a ghost! / It is I

left.text: But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid.”

right.text: And God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM”; and He said, “Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel, ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

lines.text: In Greek 'it is I' is egō eimi, literally 'I am.' The video hears in it how God identified Himself to Moses.
Egō eimi can also be an ordinary 'it's me.' On the sea, after a feeding in the wilderness, many readers hear more.

src.text: And when they got into the boat, the wind stopped. And those who were in the boat worshiped Him, saying, “You are truly God’s Son!”

lines.text: This is the first time the disciples use the title Son of God for their Rabbi. Yet Mark adds that 'they had not gained any insight about the loaves, but their heart was hardened' (Mark 6:52).

IAM.title: Do not fear; the sea is split

left.text: But Moses said to the people, “Do not fear! Stand by and see the salvation of Yahweh which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians whom you have seen today, you will never see them again forever.

right.text: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and Yahweh swept the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea into dry ground, so the waters were split.

lines.text: Moses exerted control over the chaotic sea by the power of God; Jesus as the new Moses exerts the same control. Moses says 'Do not fear!' and Jesus says 'do not be afraid' (14:27).
At the end of Exodus 14 the people 'believed in Yahweh and in His servant Moses' (Exodus 14:31); in the boat the disciples worship Jesus.

IAM.title: Your way was in the sea

src.text: Your way was in the sea / And Your paths in the mighty waters, / But Your footprints were not known. / You led Your people like a flock / By the hand of Moses and Aaron.

lines.text: Asaph describes the Exodus with God Himself present, walking a path through the sea, while Moses leads the people. It is not merely that Jesus is the new Moses: He is also the God who controls the water.

src.text: Who alone stretches out the heavens / And tramples down the waves of the sea;

lines.text: The Old Testament describes God as the one who walks on top of the sea, and 'alone.' The disciples are seeing this with their own eyes.

left.text: and they were pleading with Him that they might just touch the fringe of His garment; and as many as touched it were cured.

right.text: “But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings; and you will go forth and skip about like calves from the stall.

lines.text: The people want to do what the hemorrhaging woman did (9:20-21). The video says Malachi 4:2 led people to expect healing from the Messiah's 'wings,' an idiom for the corners of a garment where the tassels hang.
The Law commanded tassels on the corners of garments to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39).

src.text: And Peter answered and said to Him, “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water.” And He said, “Come!” And getting out of the boat, Peter walked on the water and came toward Jesus.

lines.text: The video argues 'if' should read 'since': Peter is not testing who Jesus is but asking to do what his Rabbi does. Every disciple wants to be like their teacher (Luke 6:40).
With Craig Blomberg: 'Lord, since it is you, please enable me to do the same thing you are doing.' That can be the disciple's prayer for life.

src.text: But seeing the wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and took hold of him, and *said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

lines.text: Peter did not fear the water; he feared the wind. Was it the strength of the storm, or other spiritual forces on the sea? The video says we are not sure.
Then Jesus says Peter doubted: he did not trust the One who called him out of the boat.

TRUST.title: Like the surf of the sea

src.text: But he must ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. For that man ought not to expect that he will receive anything from the Lord, being a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

lines.text: James uses the same picture: the doubter is tossed by the wind like the sea Peter is sinking into.

TRUST.title: Trust Him and what He is doing

lines.text: Jesus expects His students to trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives. Whether they need food, shelter, wisdom or insight, He gives what they need, so they can trust Him.

Even when He calls Peter out of the boat, and later calls them to come and die for Him, He gives His disciples everything they need to do what He calls them to do. The video recalls Bonhoeffer's line that when Christ calls a man, He bids him come and die.

TERMS.def: The Roman night was split into four watches; the fourth ran from about 3 to 6 in the morning.
Plural of stadion, about 185 meters; John says they had rowed 25 or 30 stadia (John 6:19).
'I am,' rendered 'it is I'; the video hears God's name from Exodus 3:14. The captions write 'egoi.'
The video's theme: Jesus retells the Exodus as the prophet like Moses.
Matthew's word for disciples who trust, but not enough (6:30; 8:26; 16:8).
The tassel on the corner of a garment, commanded in Numbers 15:38.
A hint back to an Old Testament passage.

WORDS.gloss: To torment; of a boat, to buffet or batter. Look up: BDAG, βασανίζω.
To take courage, be of good cheer.
If; with the indicative it assumes the condition for the sake of argument, which is why some render it 'since.'
To doubt, waver, be of two minds.
Edge, fringe, tassel of a garment.
Wing; also the corner or skirt of a garment. Look up: BDB or HALOT, כָּנָף.

BACKGROUND.p: The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 meters below sea level, ringed by hills. Winds funnel down the valleys, especially in the evening, and can raise sudden high waves.

In 1986 a first-century fishing boat was found in the mud near Magdala: about 8 meters long and 2.3 wide, it could carry a crew of about a dozen. A boat like it helps picture the disciples rowing all night.
Jewish men wore tassels (tzitzit) on the four corners of the outer garment, with a cord of blue, to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39). Jesus wore them too.
Jews traditionally counted three night watches; Matthew and Mark use the Roman system of four (Mark 13:35).

WITNESSES.text: To teach us, that loneliness and retirement is good, when we are to pray to God.

WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 50, on 14:28. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: For he not only believed that He was able Himself to walk on the sea, but that He could lead upon it others also; and he longs to be quickly near Him.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 50, on 14:28-29. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The video reads Peter's 'if it is You' as 'since.' Greek 'if' with the indicative presents the condition as assumed for the argument, without asserting it is true. Most translations keep 'if'; Chrysostom, like the video, sees ardor and faith, not testing.

DEBATES.h: How much does 'it is I' carry?
DEBATES.p: Some read egō eimi here as a plain 'it's me.' Others, noting Job 9:8 and Psalm 77, hear the divine name. Mark's 'He was intending to pass by them' (Mark 6:48) strengthens the second reading for many.
Most see simple fear of the storm. The video suggests spiritual forces might have been in view but says we are not sure.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says the word for 'battered' describes demonic hostility in Matthew 8:6. There it describes the centurion's servant, 'paralyzed at home, fearfully tormented' (8:6), an illness; demons use the word at 8:29: 'Have You come here to torment us before the time?'

Reading Peter's 'if' as 'since' over-reads the Greek. A first-class condition assumes the statement for the argument; it does not translate as 'since,' and the context of fear (14:26) allows real uncertainty.
That many Jews believed the gateway to the underworld lay beneath the Sea of Galilee is stated without a source; we could not confirm it.
The expectation that the Messiah would heal through His tassels, drawn from Malachi 4:2, is found in later and popular teaching; the first-century evidence for it is thin.
Craig Blomberg's rendering is given as the video reports it, and the Bonhoeffer line is the video's paraphrase; we could not check either.
The captions write 'Janzerat' and 'Janzaret' for Gennesaret, 'egoi' for egō, 'Asaf' for Asaph, 'Bonhaofer' for Bonhoeffer, and 'Blombberg' for Blomberg.

QUESTIONS: Why might Jesus have sent the disciples into a storm right after feeding the crowd?
What do Exodus 14, Psalm 77 and Job 9 add to your reading of this scene?
Do you read Peter's request as testing or as wanting to be like his Teacher?
What is the 'wind' that makes you look away from Jesus?
Where is Jesus calling you 'out of the boat' right now?
How has He already given you what you need for what He is asking of you?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: What is Jesus expecting Peter to accomplish when He says 'Come'? The lesson for the original audience: Jesus expects His students to trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives. Whatever Jesus is doing, the disciples can trust that He satisfies all their needs; they had just seen the feeding of the five thousand. Whether they need food or shelter or wisdom or insight, Jesus gives His disciples what they need so they can trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives, even when He calls Peter out of the boat to walk on the water, and even when He later calls them to come and die for Him. In the midst of all of it, Jesus gives His disciples everything they need to accomplish what He is calling them to do. Lord, since it is You, please enable me to do the same thing You are doing.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): read Psalm 77 in full. Asaph starts in distress and remembers the Exodus; notice where his attention turns, then compare Peter seeing the wind.

1. Matthew 14:28-29: Lord, command me to come
   Peter Matthew 14:28-29: "And Peter answered and said to Him, “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water.” And He said, “Come!” And getting out of the boat, Peter walked on the water and came toward Jesus." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+14:28-29
   (video) The video argues 'if' should read 'since': Peter is not testing who Jesus is but asking to do what his Rabbi does. Every disciple wants to be like their teacher (Luke 6:40).
   (video) With Craig Blomberg: 'Lord, since it is you, please enable me to do the same thing you are doing.' That can be the disciple's prayer for life.
2. Matthew 14:30-31: Seeing the wind
   Doubt Matthew 14:30-31: "But seeing the wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and took hold of him, and *said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+14:30-31
   (video) Peter did not fear the water; he feared the wind. Was it the strength of the storm, or other spiritual forces on the sea? The video says we are not sure.
   (video) Then Jesus says Peter doubted: he did not trust the One who called him out of the boat.
3. James 1:6-8: Like the surf of the sea
   Double-minded James 1:6-8: "But he must ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. For that man ought not to expect that he will receive anything from the Lord, being a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=James+1:6-8
   (video) James uses the same picture: the doubter is tossed by the wind like the sea Peter is sinking into.
4. The lesson: Trust Him and what He is doing
   (video) Jesus expects His students to trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives. Whether they need food, shelter, wisdom or insight, He gives what they need, so they can trust Him.
   (video) Even when He calls Peter out of the boat, and later calls them to come and die for Him, He gives His disciples everything they need to do what He calls them to do. The video recalls Bonhoeffer's line that when Christ calls a man, He bids him come and die.

## Key people
- Jesus: Prays alone, walks on the sea, says 'it is I,' and catches Peter. [Background] Mark adds that He 'was intending to pass by them' (Mark 6:48), language used of God passing by Moses and Elijah.
- Simon Peter: Asks to come on the water, walks, fears the wind, and sinks. [Background] Only Matthew records Peter's walk on the water.
- The disciples: Terrified, then worship Him: 'You are truly God's Son!' [Background] Mark says their heart was hardened (Mark 6:52).
- The crowd: Wanted to take Him by force to make Him king (John 6:15). [Background] They expected a political deliverer.
- The people of Gennesaret: Recognize Him and bring all who were sick. [Background] The plain of Gennesaret lay on the north-west shore between Magdala and Capernaum.
- Asaph: The psalmist of Psalm 77, who describes God's path through the sea. [Background] A Levite musician in David's time; twelve psalms carry his name (Psalms 50; 73-83).

## Places [Background]
- Bethsaida: Mark says Jesus sent the disciples ahead 'to the other side to Bethsaida' (Mark 6:45).
- Capernaum: John says they were going across the sea to Capernaum (John 6:17).
- Tabgha: The traditional site of the feeding on the north-west shore.
- Gennesaret (named in the video): Where they landed and the sick touched the fringe of His garment (14:34-36).

## Key terms
- Fourth watch: The Roman night was split into four watches; the fourth ran from about 3 to 6 in the morning. [Background]
- Stadia: Plural of stadion, about 185 meters; John says they had rowed 25 or 30 stadia (John 6:19). [Background]
- Egō eimi: 'I am,' rendered 'it is I'; the video hears God's name from Exodus 3:14. The captions write 'egoi.'
- New Moses: The video's theme: Jesus retells the Exodus as the prophet like Moses.
- Little faith: Matthew's word for disciples who trust, but not enough (6:30; 8:26; 16:8).
- Fringe: The tassel on the corner of a garment, commanded in Numbers 15:38.
- Remez: A hint back to an Old Testament passage.

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- βασανίζω basanizō (G928, Greek): To torment; of a boat, to buffet or batter. Look up: BDAG, βασανίζω. (Matt 14:24)
- φάντασμα phantasma (G5326, Greek): Apparition, ghost. (Matt 14:26)
- θαρσέω tharseō (G2293, Greek): To take courage, be of good cheer. (Matt 14:27)
- εἰ ei (G1487, Greek): If; with the indicative it assumes the condition for the sake of argument, which is why some render it 'since.' (Matt 14:28)
- ὀλιγόπιστος oligopistos (G3640, Greek): Of little faith. (Matt 14:31)
- διστάζω distazō (G1365, Greek): To doubt, waver, be of two minds. (Matt 14:31)
- κράσπεδον kraspedon (G2899, Greek): Edge, fringe, tassel of a garment. (Matt 14:36)
- כָּנָף kanaph (H3671, Hebrew): Wing; also the corner or skirt of a garment. Look up: BDB or HALOT, כָּנָף. (Mal 4:2)
- דָּרַךְ darak (H1869, Hebrew): To tread, trample, march. (Job 9:8)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Storms on the lake: The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 meters below sea level, ringed by hills. Winds funnel down the valleys, especially in the evening, and can raise sudden high waves.
- The Galilee boat: In 1986 a first-century fishing boat was found in the mud near Magdala: about 8 meters long and 2.3 wide, it could carry a crew of about a dozen. A boat like it helps picture the disciples rowing all night.
- Tassels: Jewish men wore tassels (tzitzit) on the four corners of the outer garment, with a cord of blue, to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:38-39). Jesus wore them too.
- Night watches: Jews traditionally counted three night watches; Matthew and Mark use the Roman system of four (Mark 13:35).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'If' or 'since'? The video reads Peter's 'if it is You' as 'since.' Greek 'if' with the indicative presents the condition as assumed for the argument, without asserting it is true. Most translations keep 'if'; Chrysostom, like the video, sees ardor and faith, not testing.
- How much does 'it is I' carry? Some read egō eimi here as a plain 'it's me.' Others, noting Job 9:8 and Psalm 77, hear the divine name. Mark's 'He was intending to pass by them' (Mark 6:48) strengthens the second reading for many.
- What did Peter fear? Most see simple fear of the storm. The video suggests spiritual forces might have been in view but says we are not sure.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says the word for 'battered' describes demonic hostility in Matthew 8:6. There it describes the centurion's servant, 'paralyzed at home, fearfully tormented' (8:6), an illness; demons use the word at 8:29: 'Have You come here to torment us before the time?'
- Reading Peter's 'if' as 'since' over-reads the Greek. A first-class condition assumes the statement for the argument; it does not translate as 'since,' and the context of fear (14:26) allows real uncertainty.
- That many Jews believed the gateway to the underworld lay beneath the Sea of Galilee is stated without a source; we could not confirm it.
- The expectation that the Messiah would heal through His tassels, drawn from Malachi 4:2, is found in later and popular teaching; the first-century evidence for it is thin.
- Craig Blomberg's rendering is given as the video reports it, and the Bonhoeffer line is the video's paraphrase; we could not check either.
- The captions write 'Janzerat' and 'Janzaret' for Gennesaret, 'egoi' for egō, 'Asaf' for Asaph, 'Bonhaofer' for Bonhoeffer, and 'Blombberg' for Blomberg.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why might Jesus have sent the disciples into a storm right after feeding the crowd?
2. What do Exodus 14, Psalm 77 and Job 9 add to your reading of this scene?
3. Do you read Peter's request as testing or as wanting to be like his Teacher?
4. What is the 'wind' that makes you look away from Jesus?
5. Where is Jesus calling you 'out of the boat' right now?
6. How has He already given you what you need for what He is asking of you?

## Application
- (video) What is Jesus expecting Peter to accomplish when He says 'Come'? The lesson for the original audience: Jesus expects His students to trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives. Whatever Jesus is doing, the disciples can trust that He satisfies all their needs; they had just seen the feeding of the five thousand. Whether they need food or shelter or wisdom or insight, Jesus gives His disciples what they need so they can trust Him and what He is doing in and through their lives, even when He calls Peter out of the boat to walk on the water, and even when He later calls them to come and die for Him. In the midst of all of it, Jesus gives His disciples everything they need to accomplish what He is calling them to do. Lord, since it is You, please enable me to do the same thing You are doing.
- Study note (added): read Psalm 77 in full. Asaph starts in distress and remembers the Exodus; notice where his attention turns, then compare Peter seeing the wind.
